dasārahā.notes: SN 20.7 names the Dasārahas as the owners of the Ānaka drum. The page citation also picks up SN 20.6, whose simile concerns four archers.

daṇḍakappaka.notes: AN 6.62 names the Kosalan town and the Aciravatī. A monk asks Ānanda about the Buddha’s declaration concerning Devadatta, and Ānanda relays his question. The entry calls this the Udānasutta. The app titles it Purisindriyañāṇasutta. AN 6.61 shares the cited page and is set at Isipatana near Varanasi.

devadaha.notes: MN 101, SN 22.2 and SN 35.134 each explicitly call Devadaha a Sakyan town. SN 22.1 takes place among the Bhaggas and shares the cited page with SN 22.2. The entry’s abbreviated second SN reference, iv.124f, reaches SN 35.134 on page 125, but the packet’s citation list omits it.

devadatta.notes: SN 17.31 names Devadatta as the monk who split the Saṅgha. Check the entry’s claim that Ud 1.5 praises him among eleven elders. The app’s Pali and English at Ud 1.5:1.3 list ten, ending with Nanda, and omit Devadatta. MN 58 quotes the prediction of his fate. The refusal to hand him the Saṅgha is a different episode. Candikāputta reports his teaching in AN 9.26. AN 9.25 shares the page. The citation list misses AN 6.62, AN 4.68 and AN 8.7, corresponding to the entry’s abbreviated AN references 402, ii.73 and iv.160. The matches in AN 4.70, AN 8.10 and SN 6.15 occur only in closing verse indexes.

devahita.notes: SN 7.13 names Devahita as the brahmin who supplies hot water and molasses for the Buddha. SN 7.12 concerns Udaya and shares the cited page. At AN 8.38:5.3, devahito means ‘good for the gods’, parallel to ‘good for the king’. A tap there would incorrectly identify the brahmin. SN 7.22:4.1 names Devahita only in the chapter’s closing verse index.
